en: O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, Protector of the World, Master of the Universe!
You have taught the mantra-tantra in detail, together with the means for accomplishing the essential reality.
But these mortals have short lifespans, little vigor, and small intelligence;
they possess little strength of character and meager wealth, and are possessed by greed and delusion.
O Lord, for the sake of my favor, you ought to speak that which is concise in words yet vast in meaning, and which is filled with the hosts of categories of reality, for the benefit of these gods.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim this scripture, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain,
extracted like clarified butter from curd from the Vātula Tantra.
That supreme seed known as Nāda, which resides within all beings,
is the highest bestower of liberation and the granter of divine accomplishments.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, one becomes a teacher and a destroyer of bonds;
even cowherds, women, children, barbarians, and those who speak common vernaculars [attain this].
Even the beings dwelling within the water constantly speak of him;
having understood that which is gross, subtle, and supreme, one should perform whatever action is desired.
The gross is said to be sound; the subtle consists of thought;
that which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the supreme.
It is peaceful, all-pervading, and empty, abiding within the twelve measures.
O Six-faced One, the short vowels are said to be the Brahmās, while the long ones are the limbs.
The anusvāra, situated above all [the letters], becomes the eye;
that which is accompanied by the visarga and devoid of the anusvāra becomes the weapon (astra).
One should join the sixth [vowel] with the end of the thirteenth [consonant] in the fifth [syllable];
one should know that to be Śiva, the Sadāśiva who is the embodiment of mantra.
The second of the sixth [syllable] is joined with the first of the fourth;
then one should again join the first [syllable] from the fifth of the second.
With the Śiva-weapon [consisting of] the crest[-mantra], one destroys obstacles; it is remembered as the bestower of liberation.
This divine Pāśupata [mantra] severs all bonds.
The Brahma-mantras, Śiva with his limbs (aṅgas), the Netra, and the Pāśupata—
this entire auspicious extraction of mantras has been told by you in brief.
I shall now proclaim its mudrā for the benefit of practitioners:
with both hands, one should touch [the body] from the feet upward as far as the head. (Stk 1.15)
This is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), which accomplishes all desires and purposes;
having first performed the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa), one should then form the seal-binding.
One should purify the soles of the feet and the backs of the hands with the weapon seed-syllable;
beginning with the little finger and ending with the thumb.
One should carefully place the Brahma-mantras there, as well as the ancillary limbs (aṅgas);
afterwards, one should place the pervasive temple (prāsāda), which faces in all directions.
The first chapter:
The arrangement of the internal organ and likewise the purification of the elements.
Having first performed the purification of the elements, one should then perform the arrangement of the internal organ.
One should sequentially hold the seed-syllable of the heart conjoined with the earth element for the earth [tattva];
the head-mantra in water; the crest-mantra in fire; and the armor-mantra together with air.
One should always hold the weapon-mantra joined with Śiva, namely Ākāśa, ending with *huṃ phaṭ*; having especially pierced the membrane, one should ascend upwards. (Stk 2.3)
There are five upward thrusts, and four, three, two, and even one;
at the end of the twelve, consciousness remains alone, without support.
O child, one should perform the ritual application according to the procedure for initiation;
then, one should contemplate the nectar situated within the process (prakriyā) as flowing forth.
By means of the syllable *oṃ*, there then arises the lotus, the seat of yoga, resembling the solar disc; indeed, it is the letter *a*, born from the self.
The *vidyātattva* is the letter *u*, while the *śivatattva* is born from the letter *m*;
it consists of the *puryaṣṭaka*, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), which is Sadāśiva.
One should contemplate the supreme abode, which pierces the crown of the head via the *suṣumnā*;
by that [light], one should contemplate oneself as being completely flooded and fully filled.
For that mortal who recites this samādhi which destroys death, death does not arise; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Thereafter, the reception of the Guru, the practitioners, and the image should take place;
one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), beginning from the head, starting with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
Having offered the eye and invoked him, the wise one should then contemplate Sadāśiva, the God of gods, as the omniscient Self.
The knower of mantras should place the heart, the head, the crest-lock, the armor, and the weapon in their respective locations in due order.
One should perform the rite of worship in the heart and arrange the fire-oblation at the navel;
one should meditate upon the Lord, the granter of boons, facing in all directions, in the forehead.
As it is in worship, so it is in the fire; as it is in meditation, so it is likewise in bathing.
The wise one should contemplate that as it is with the deity, so it is with his own body.
O Six-faced One, having thus first prepared the internal organ,
and afterwards the external [organ], one should then commence the sacrifice after making both the internal and external [pure].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Arrangement of the Internal Organ.
Hereafter, I shall explain the auspicious bath that removes all sins.
Having gathered earth with the *astra* mantra recited once, the knower of mantras [should proceed].
Having first performed the ritual bath with earth and having recited the Saṃhitā once,
one should thereafter consecrate that very same earth by reciting [the mantra] over it once for each application.
Then, having divided it into three portions, one should consecrate the first with the Astra-mantra;
the second, O child, with the Brahma-mantras; and the third with the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform the binding of the directions with a portion consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
the holy site (tīrtha) with one consecrated by the Śiva-mantra, and the body (vigraha) with one consecrated by the Brahma-mantra.
Then, having whetted [the razor], one should bathe in the midst of the Śivatīrtha with the ritual honors due to a universal monarch,
using fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and other such substances.
Having sipped water according to the rule, the practitioner should worship the twilight;
O child, he should perform the ritual attendance with all the mantras once.
Having first performed the consecration, one should then perform the twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*);
one should not apply the weapon-mantra (*astra*) to the body, but should cast it only outside.
O child, one should wither the body so that it is no longer joined to the self;
rather, the wise should always employ it amidst obstacles and the snares of bondage.
Then, with his heart, the wise one should satisfy the ancestors and the gods;
he should perform the withdrawal of that sacred site by means of the *prāsāda* mantra alone.
The third chapter, titled "The Section on the Varuṇa Bath.
O Six-faced One, hereafter I shall explain the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*):
having consecrated the ashes once with all the mantras in their proper sequence, [one should proceed].
O Six-faced One, having first performed the ritual bath with water using the Astra-bīja,
the knower of mantras should then perform the formal bath (vidhisnāna), beginning from the head.
One should bathe the head with Īśāna, the face with Tatpuruṣa,
the heart with Bahurūpa, and the private parts with Guhyaka.
O Six-faced One, one should perform the sprinkling of all limbs with the Unborn [mantra], the consecration with the five [mantras], and the bath with the Prasāda [mantra] above.
The fourth chapter, titled "The Section on the Ash-Bath," concludes here.
Now I shall fully explain the ritual worship according to the rules and in their proper sequence.
First, the seed and sprout by means of power; afterwards, the infinite seat.
O Six-faced One, one should gradually bring the infinite to its end;
[the sequence is] the heart, the pericarp, the lotus, and likewise Dharma, Jñāna, and the others.
One should place detachment and likewise sovereignty, ending with the Lord (Īśa), starting from the fire [quarter];
and one should fashion the arrangement of filaments with the powers and the heart-mantra.
Then, O Six-faced One, one should invoke the deity with the heart-mantra;
likewise, one should perform the rites of installation, the offering of water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and the sipping of water.
One should perform both the ceremonial bathing and the worship with the Heart-mantra;
whatever has been mentioned or left unsaid, all that should be done with the Heart-mantra.
This single protection accomplishes all desired aims;
it is common to all tantras and supreme among all forms of knowledge.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Section on Sacrifice," is concluded.
Hereafter, I shall explain the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya) in its proper sequence.
One should perform the sweeping with the Astra-mantra and then the sprinkling with the Varma-mantra.
Then, one should perform the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa) with darbha grass using the Heart mantra alone;
indeed, with the Heart mantra, one should cast the fire (jātavedas) into the womb of power.
Having performed the rites beginning with the conception ceremony (garbhādhāna) and the final expiation,
the knower of mantras should perform all ritual acts using the heart-mantra alone.
Thereafter, one should arrange the previously described lotus diagram and perform the fire oblation (homa) with all the mantras, beginning with Śiva, in their proper sequence.
The sixth chapter, titled "The Section on the Fire-Rite," concludes here.
Hereafter, I shall explain the mandala that fulfills all desires.
Having purified the ground by means of the ritual prescribed in the treatises, one should proceed.
Then, having given his consent under an asterism presided over by Jupiter,
the wise one should draw the auspicious maṇḍala that bestows all accomplishments.
Having measured it out perfectly with a cord so that it is square on all sides,
one should place a lotus in the center, possessing eight petals and a pericarp.
A wise person should draw the three enclosures, measuring one cubit, two cubits, or even four cubits, as prescribed in the independent [tantras].
The preceptor, being well-composed, should cause the western gate to be opened;
he should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed in the southeast, measuring one cubit in size.
One should perform the ritual procedure for the sacrifice in a well-kindled fire;
beginning from the east, one should install the faces and the other [limbs] in their proper sequence.
Having first deposited the purifiers, one should then deposit the limbs of Śiva:
having deposited the heart in the southeast, one should likewise deposit the head in the northeast.
The *śikhā* is to be known in the southwest, and the *kavaca* in the domain of the wind (the northwest);
having then assigned the *astra* to the directions, one should place Sadāśiva upon the pericarp.
The procedure for the deposition of the embryo has been declared; now hear concerning the second enclosure.
Beginning first with the heart-mantra, one should worship the world-protectors.
[In the third enclosure, one should worship the weapons with their respective mantras.
O Skanda, I have thus briefly proclaimed the ritual procedure. Stk_7.10 //
Whatever may be left unsaid, all that should be based upon the root [text].
Thus, one who knows the rules and procedures should perform the rite of initiation.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on the Ritual of the Maṇḍala.
Now, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā) as it is established in the five principles (pañcatattva).
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well.
These five principles pervade the entire world;
therefore, all principles whatsoever should be perceived by practitioners as being contained within them alone.
In the Brahmāṇḍa, however, Nivṛtti extends up to the limit of the Śatarudras;
above that, Pratiṣṭhā exists as far as the realm of the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Then that Vidyā was dispatched to the presence of the Lord of Vidyās;
thereafter, peace prevails in the end of the path, for in the state of Śiva there is only Śakti.
He who desires to perform initiation without knowing these principles undergoes fruitless labor; he shall certainly not obtain its fruit.
Cessation should be known as earth; water is called the foundation.
One should understand fire as knowledge; wind is proclaimed to be peace.
Beyond Peace is Space; it is the supreme, peaceful, and imperishable.
Having known that, O Mahāsena, one may initiate even outcastes.
The Guru [should place] Nivṛtti with the heart, Pratiṣṭhā with the head,
Śiva with the crest-lock (śikhā), and Śānti with the armor (kavaca).
One should perform the fire oblation with the *prāsāda* mantra into the supreme void beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*);
one hundred oblations for each [deity], and thus one should perform five such oblations.
O Six-faced One, one should offer five full oblations with the Prāsāda mantra for the sake of purification through expiation,
and eight oblations with each [of the other mantras].
The knower of mantras should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in due order using the seed-syllable of the weapon;
in this way, initiation is completed, being devoid of birth and the like.
By means of the oblation alone, practitioners are liberated from the bondage of birth;
this rite must not be disclosed, but kept secret with great effort.
This is the secret of all tantras, the supreme consecration; it includes the ritual placement upon the womb (yoninyāsa) and other rites, as well as the extraction [of mantras], which is unsurpassed.
O God, explain the sequence of purification according to the rule;
O Guha, you have asked here about those seventeen who are to be purified.
I shall now describe, in due order, that which has been stated as the seed-syllable for each;
one should likewise assign the seed-syllable of the womb to the heart according to the sequence.
Worship, sprinkling, and likewise striking,
as well as joining, union, and immediately thereafter, depositing.
Then one should perform worship, as well as the rites of conception,
birth, qualification, enjoyment, and likewise dissolution.
O Six-faced One, one should offer a hundred oblations into the self-nature with the heart-mantra;
likewise, one should perform the severing of the bonds with the weapon-mantra, and then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In this case, the extraction must be performed by means of the heart-mantra according to the proper sequence;
likewise for the sprinkling and the striking.
One should perform [the ritual] in successive order, joined with the syllables *hum* and *phaṭ*;
furthermore, the reconnection of the principles (*tattvas*) must be performed according to their proper sequence.
In each and every reality, this is the ritual action and this indeed is the sequence of the procedure;
once these have been purified, my child, one attains the complete rite.
Otherwise, O Six-faced One, those who lack the prescribed ritual do not attain liberation at all;
therefore, the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) must be performed accompanied by mental concentration (dhāraṇā).
O child, one should mentally contemplate the supreme nectar as it flows;
for this is to be applied everywhere and at all times within the section concerning initiation.
O sinless one, regarding the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga* and the rites of constant purification, you previously spoke of the seizing and releasing of the animal (*paśu*).
Where are the internal and external fetters situated in the body?
In what place are they to be severed, and how does immediate departure [from the body] occur?
O Maheśvara, tell us the instruction regarding the sacrificial animals,
having grasped the first with the second by means of the self through the self.
The wise one should lead that [subtle body] to its respective location by means of the fist;
through the application of the equinox (viṣuvat), those [deities] beginning with Brahmā and ending with Śiva [are attained].
In one case they attain equality, but otherwise they remain separate;
at the end of the twelve, however, they are to be severed by means of an arrow joined with a weapon-mantra.
Then they attain union, freed from all conventional observances;
yet whatever is performed that is unindicated and nameless shall be in vain.
Any action performed with that as its object bestows liberation; of this there is no doubt, O child, especially during a solar eclipse conjoined with the Viṣuvat yoga.
When it is severed at the end of its length, it certainly departs;
the snares knotted within the mind are like clusters of gems upon a thread.
Seeing that the mind is spread out like a web of threads extending from the heart-lotus to that [supreme] lotus,
one should effect its cutting by means of the mental faculty through the severing of the mind.
When the mind is severed within the mind, the individual soul attains absolute isolation.
O Lord of Gods, abandon prolixity; speak to me in brief.
By the mere knowledge of which one liberates the bound souls (paśus) in an instant.
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the truth by which liberation will certainly be attained.
The knower of mantras, by means of an extremely subtle application perceived through yoga,
should impel that Śakti by way of the divine path of yoga.
Having known that living being to consist of vital breath, O Mahāsena, the wise one should,
through the application of the equinox, unite it with the eternal state.
But having attained the yoga of the equinox, who would not be liberated from bondage?
[One should contemplate] the lotus-channels of the earth and other elements, together with the winds possessing qualities such as sound.
Having known the mantras whose presiding deity is the Self, one who is liberated can liberate others.
Indeed, the openings of the channels are connected, having upward stalks and downward-facing mouths.
All [the syllables], joined with the two knots and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, then ascend upwards by means of the upward thrusts (*udghāta*), O Guha, as before. (Stk 8.39)
Having again observed the earth and the other elements with the mind, both internally and externally,
they should be applied to their respective principles, divested [of attachment] and free from egoism.
O child, one should cause Brahmā and the others to hear [this]; one shall not undergo rebirth again.
Having practiced the fire-essence and the mind twice, there is the expansion of the sun.
Having struck it first, O child, the seizing should take place as before.
Having broken the bolt, one should place the *yoni*; one should join the principle (*tattva*) with the principle.
Having encapsulated it with the *śaktis*, one should deposit it with the ending *vauṣaṭ*.
The eighth chapter, concerning initiation, [ends here].
Now I shall proclaim the consecration, not in detail but in brief,
as spoken by the Supreme Lord for the benefit of the foremost of practitioners.
Indeed, one should take a single earthen jar smeared with sandalwood paste,
or else a vessel made of *brahmapatra* leaves, or even a vessel made of lotus leaves.
Having prepared it with all medicinal herbs and adorned with all fragrances,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times for the temple facing in all directions.

Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should then cause the consecration to be performed on an auspicious lunar mansion day, at a favorable moment (muhūrta) endowed with the proper astrological conditions (karaṇa).
Amidst the sounds of many auspicious proclamations, the resonance of conchs and cymbals,
various Vedic chants accompanied by dance and song,
the preceptor, having been authorized and consecrated, shall become a destroyer of bonds.
The ninth chapter on consecration:
I shall now explain, in due order, the supreme and most subtle wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*). From the bulbous root (*kanda*) situated below the navel, sprouts emerge.
Seventy-two thousand [channels] are situated in the center of the navel;
they pervade everywhere from the navel—sideways, upwards, and downwards.
The principal channels are arranged like the spokes of a wheel; among them, there are ten, of which the first three are the iḍā, the piṅgalā, and the third, the suṣumnā.
Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, Yaśas,
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, and Śaṅkhinī is remembered as the tenth.
These ten channels are proclaimed as the carriers of the vital breaths:
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
The Nāga, the Kūrma, the Kṛkara, the Devadatta, and the Dhanañjaya;
the Prāṇa is the first wind, and it is the lord of all nine.
The vital breath is the "breath-made" (prāṇamaya); the vital breath is the emission directed toward filling.
Abiding in the chest of living beings, it constantly fills them.
Because the vital breath (prāṇa), which is dependent upon the individual soul (jīva), performs the act of departing through exhalation, inhalation, and coughing,
it is therefore proclaimed as "prāṇa."
The apāna wind, however, leads food downward in men;
because this wind carries away urine, semen, and waste, it is called apāna.
When drunk, eaten, or smelled, it [cures] blood-bile,
phlegm, wind,
and so forth.
According to Sanderson (lecture notes on the *Tantrasāra*):
"The wind named Samāna leads [the vital breath] equally throughout the limbs."
The wind named udāna causes the lower lip to quiver, agitates the face, eyes, and limbs, and disturbs the vital points (marmas). Stk 10.11.
Vyāna distorts the limbs; vyāna provokes disease;
it causes the destruction of pleasure; because it pervades (vyāpana), it is called vyāna.
Nāga is said to be in the belching; Kūrma is remembered in the opening of the eyes; Kṛkara is in the sneeze, and Devadatta in the yawning;
Dhanañjaya resides in the sound [of digestion] and does not leave even when one has died.

This very collection of winds, placed within the heart and established in the navel-cakra, breathes through inhalations and exhalations; by its downward throbbing and whirling, it constantly causes the city of the body to tremble.
Ever producing slight births, this single wind torments the beast [of a being] in childhood and youth; seized by birth and death, it sports with deluded sentient beings.
I shall explain the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra) according to its actual state in proper sequence,
and how the division of this ten-spoked wheel arises.
This living being revolves like a wheel through the ten stations in succession;
though he is the life-force of the world of living beings, those who are deluded do not perceive him at all.
The individual soul (jīva) moves through ten ways; therefore, it is proclaimed as a "wheel" (cakra).
It is called the "wheel of channels" (nāḍīcakra) because by means of it the soul indeed transmigrates.
In the center of the sky of the heart is an eight-petaled lotus, and within it is its pericarp;
in the heart-lotus are the powers (śaktis) possessing the radiance of the sun, moon, fire, and gold.
What meter is this? The answer is *Anuṣṭubh*.The answer is *Anuṣṭubh*. I hope it is correct.
The noble one (Āryā) is bad because of [her] transmission.
Indeed, Śakti was formerly the one who moves above them; therefore, she is Śiva’s.
Like a bee, that Puruṣa is dissolved in the midst of the lotus of the fourfold Śaktis. (Stk 10.19)
For when the instruments of the senses are grasped by the pincers of the wind of emptiness on both sides, they move along wherever they are led, like dry leaves carried by the wind. (Āryā 10.20)
Confined by the noose consisting of the four digits (*kalā*), it wanders within the lotus;
like a ball struck with ease, it performs leaping up and falling down.
Through union with the Lord (*īśvara*) and the equinox (*viṣuvat*), as well as through connection with the supernatural powers (*siddhi*), [it attains liberation].
The southern course is due to conjunction with the sun, and the northern course is due to conjunction with the moon.
The two nostril-paths, moving to the left and right, are called the solstices;
because it moves from here and there, it is designated as the *saṃkrānti* (transition).
The solar [path] is declared to be the left course, while the lunar is the other.
Indeed, the solar moon is auspicious for the conjunction with fire.
He who is established on the eastern petal during the equinox through meditation and so forth would become a king, free from pride.
If [the breath] moves in the petal belonging to the direction of Agni, there arises brilliance, or the affliction of hunger. (Stk 10.25)
In the south, the southern disposition is indicated;
in the southwest,
the southwestern [disposition] is specified.

On a leaf of Varuṇa, it becomes Varuṇa; on a leaf of Marut, it attains the state of Marut. On a leaf of Soma, it is said to be of the nature of Soma, and on a leaf of Īśa, it is of the nature of Īśa. Whichever direction it approaches, it completely assumes the nature of that [deity].
Because of the union with the intermediate spaces between the petals, the self then appears as if empty.
Thus, indeed, the movement of the person (*pudgala*) is the primary mandala of the arrangement of the channels;
this which has been explained here as the cause of accomplishment should be understood with effort once it is mastered. (Stk 10.28)
The tenth chapter: On the Network of Channels (Nāḍīcakra).

O Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, that life-force (*jīva*) is known as moving within the self (*adhyātma*) just like [the breath] of the world of living beings; I have a great doubt—be gracious to me.
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the vision of the living being called Puruṣa;
I shall describe it to you without a doubt, especially out of affection for my son.
The transits and the equinoxes, as well as the days, nights, and solstices;
the intercalary month and debt, and likewise the omitted night and wealth.
A sneeze should be known as a deficient night (ūnarātra), and yawning as an intercalary month (adhimāsa).
Coughing should be understood as debt, while sighing is said to be wealth.
The northern [channel] is to be known as the right, situated on the left and right;
however, that which issues forth from both nostrils is declared to be the equinox (viṣuvat) in the middle.
Furthermore, its transference (saṃkrānti) occurs from its own place to another place;
these are Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Amā as the third.
The Suṣumnā is indeed proclaimed to be in the central limb, the Iḍā in the left, and the Piṅgalā in the right limb; the transition among these is now described.

The upward-moving breath (prāṇa) is indeed declared to be day, and the downward-moving breath (apāna) is said to be night. He who knows these ten divisions of the breath is truly a knower of the Veda. (Stk 11.8)
The extension situated within the center of the body is considered to be the lunar eclipse;
however, the wise one should know that which transcends the body to be the solar eclipse.
In a single day and night, that lord of yogis performs a recitation numbering twenty-two thousand six hundred.
I shall explain to you in brief the entirety of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The knower of yoga should utter the Praṇava with a single tone.
Having filled the abdomen with air as much as desired, this is *prāṇāyāma*; it is called *pūraka* because it fills the body.
Having closed all the gates [of the senses] and being free from inhalation and exhalation, one should remain like a completely filled jar; that is *prāṇāyāma*, known as *kumbhaka*.
Then the knower of yoga, joined with the practice of exhalation, should release the breath upwards with a single breath,
exhaling as far as it reaches upward.
This is known as *recaka*, which causes the cessation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
it is that lotus which always remains situated in the heart with its face turned downward.
Filled by means of inhalation (pūraka), this [lotus] blooms above;
by means of retention (kumbhaka), the upward-flowing lotus becomes obstructed.
Likewise, when cast out by the *recaka* breath— which instantly robs one of life—
it leaves the heart-lotus and becomes established in the upward flow (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
For when exhaled, it goes upward, piercing the knot in an instant;
having pierced the opening of the skull, the life-force (jīva), being exhaled, indeed ascends.
Having attained the state of Sadāśiva, one shall not undergo birth again;
for him alone, and never for anyone else, is the *āyāma* performed.
Thus have I briefly described that life-force (*jīva*) of the world of living beings.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter:
"The primordial Kuṇḍalinī, joined like the moon and fire,
should be known to reside in the region of the heart, situated in the form of a sprout."
There, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the method of emanation, as taught in the section on the double repetition;
the best of practitioners should contemplate nectar flowing therefrom.
One who desires spiritual accomplishment should, with a concentrated mind, contemplate the entire world— both stationary and moving— as consisting of Agni and Soma, yet in their reversed forms.
The wise one should contemplate his own body as having a divine form beyond compare;
he should contemplate whatever specific action has been prescribed for him.
And whoever should practice this nectar that faces in all directions,
in a very short time they shall become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment.
Without knowing the ritual placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), how can the practitioner apply it?
He would be like one striking at empty space with his fists or threshing chaff.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the emanation of the mantra-script in its proper sequence,
and how the deity with parts (sakala) is endowed with the partless (niṣkala).
He produced the *kalā* that sets all mantras in motion;
situated in the middle upon the head of the syllable *oṃ*, it likewise pervades the syllable *oṃ*.
The Lord creates the first line as the syllable Oṃ;
that indeed is the digit called Vidyā, which is established in every phoneme.
The line that is clearly visible when the letter *u* is superimposed upon the syllable *oṃ* should be known as "Pratiṣṭhā," arising from the phoneme *u*.
That subtle, stainless line which exists upon its summit became the letter *Ma*; that is the power (*kalā*) known as Nivṛtti.
United with the summit of the syllable Oṃ, it dissolves at the summit of the syllable Oṃ;
this line in the void is Nirvāṇa, and that digit is called Peace (śānti).
Through conjunction, she shines forth, abiding both in the partless and in the possessed-of-parts;
when the *oṃkāra* is ascended upon the crown of the head, sound is born therein.
That power is considered supreme and subtle, accompanied by the *bindu*,
like the great light of a lamp together with its sparks and flames.
As it falls, it proceeds in three ways according to the nature of Śiva’s powers (vidyās);
these are the kalās known as Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti.
The digit (kalā) that falls there as a line together with the point (bindu),
along with Vidyeshvara, is declared to be Śiva, the God of gods, Sadāśiva.
First, its seed is said to be the *nāda* and the *bindu*;
it does not abandon the supreme station, which is eternal, fixed, and imperishable.
Having cast the drop into its interior, it protects it like a mother;
above that, on the left side, the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu is established.
The southern [line], situated at the source of Brahmā, exists as one alone yet established in three ways;
that central line is endowed with two side-bindus.
Therein dwells the subtle Lord Śiva, the auspicious Śaṅkara, hidden;
that supreme deity is the seed, Maheśvara, whose womb is Śakti.
From which proceeds the entire system of mantra and tantra, including all that is moving and unmoving—
that which is unmanifest, supreme, subtle, the stainless embodiment of power.
Śiva is without beginning or end; by knowing him, one is not born again.
For that seed which resides in the south is indeed the supreme power of knowledge (jñānaśakti).
That seed-syllable is the supreme Brahman, wherein He remains hidden;
it is the leftward-moving supreme point (bindu), for that is indeed the supreme power of action (kriyā-śakti).
In that regard, Viṣṇu himself is subtle, stainless, and hidden within the seed;
this very deity, though established in creation, was emitted by Śambhu.
Because it is hidden, they do not perceive that by which the moving and the unmoving were created;
from his emission (visarga) creation is born—he alone is the Lord, the Sovereign.
Because that seed was emitted by him, it is called "visarga" (emission);
and by that [seed], this entire world is filled and consists of that very essence.
By means of a multitude of rays of power, hundreds and thousands of times over,
he— acting as the uniter and the disuniter— indeed emits and reabsorbs [all things].
And by means of the power of knowledge, the Lord Śiva indeed bestows grace;
from *visarga* comes creation, while dissolution occurs together with the *bindu*.
Nirvāṇa is the realization of reality, which is the domain of the expansion of the Tantra.
O Lord, the section on the emanation of mantras, as well as both dissolution and emanation, has all been declared;
now tell me in brief about the loss of the destination for those who have been initiated.

O Six-faced One, listen to that reality regarding the yoga that causes the loss of one's state when it is deceptive, treacherous, cruel, devoid of essence, fond of quarrel, and destructive of one's progress.
Having performed this, one should gradually fix the gaze upon the moon placed at the crown of the head; having mentally observed its movement as before, one should then withdraw it.
O Six-faced One, having first and last performed the *saṃhārasampuṭa* *kūṭa*,
one should offer a hundred oblations for each individual letter of the *mātṛkā* separately.
Chapter on the Loss of the State:
The man who, engaged in yoga, constantly recites [the mantra] after having raised the sound of the *prāsāda*, shall attain perfection within six months; of this there is no doubt.
For one who recites [the mantra] while walking back and forth, there shall be the destruction of all sins;
within six months, one will undoubtedly attain the sovereign power of the qualities such as *aṇimā*.
Having understood the coming and going, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Becoming absorbed in that and merged with it, one shall attain perfection within six months.
The gross, the subtle, and the supreme Prāsāda have been described by me;
those who do not understand the Prāsāda do not understand Śaṅkara.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the section on the classification of temples and the characteristics of a temple;
the knower of mantras should always discern whether it is short, long, or protracted.
The short [form] burns away sins; the long [form] becomes the bestower of liberation;
the prolated [form] serves for nourishment, adorned with a bindu upon the head.

The three gross divisions are said to be subjugation (*vaśya*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). By means of the *pluta* [vowel], one always effects subjugation; there is no doubt in this matter.
A long [syllable] will swiftly expel [the enemy] by means of the syllable *phaṭ*; of this there is no doubt.
For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), the short *phaṭ* is prescribed at both the beginning and the end.
The heart-mantra is taught for use at the beginning and the end during the rite of summoning;
when properly employed, it will certainly summon even one situated a hundred yojanas away.
Thus one should attract the object of practice after truly understanding its name;
it is taught that the [syllables] of the practitioner should be many, while those of the object of practice should be few.
Having understood this, the wise person certainly performs the extraction;
however, without correctly understanding this, it never succeeds at all.
Having performed the sacrifice as previously described, one should cause the *arghya* for the mantra to be offered.
Having offered the *arghya*, the wise practitioner should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra.
One should perform the recitation for five hundred thousand times, standing on the right side of the deity;
at the conclusion of the recitation, there should be an oblation of ghee performed ten thousand times.
When the mantra has been thus nourished, it then becomes fit for ritual action;
there is no doubt that the rites, whether explicitly mentioned or not, will attain success.
For those who recite it one million times while residing in their own place, the people will swiftly come under their control; such is the certainty of the scripture.
For one who recites three million five hundred thousand times while residing in ten villages,
those people come under one's control, both in person and through their wealth.
O Six-faced One, by means of twenty lakhs [of recitations] for the temple,
the mantra-practitioner will certainly bring the lords of various regions under his control.
By twenty-five hundred thousand recitations, one shall bring the object under control;
by thirty hundred thousand recitations, the mandala itself shall indeed be brought under control.
By reciting it three million five hundred thousand times, one shall bring the earth under one's control;
by forty million recitations, one beholds the god Hāṭakeśvara.
Having recited [the mantra] five million times, the practitioner of mantra becomes equal to a vidyādhara;
he rejoices in that very state until the dissolution of all beings.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Characteristics of Palaces," is thus the sixteenth book.
O Lord, even now there remains a clear doubt regarding gnosis (*jñāna*) and realized knowledge (*vijñāna*).
How is knowledge known, or how is the object of knowledge described?
Having first understood the support and then that which is supported,
the wise person who knows the relationship between support and supported is competent in all activities.
The support is called the city, while that which is supported is called the Lord (Īśa). Having realized the Lord, the wise man always rejoices by himself.
Endowed with the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), it indeed moves upward and downward;
[it consists of] the pentad of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Intellect, mind, and ego—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*).
(Note: This definition of the *puryaṣṭaka* is not accepted by Rāmakaṇṭha without considerable distortion.)
As long as one has not been liberated by these, how could one be released from bondage?
One should abandon touch and sound in Brahmā; indeed, one should abandon taste in Keśava;
one should abandon form and smell in Rudra; and the intellect and ego in Īśvara.
Having abandoned the mind and the vital drop (bindu) in Śiva, one is liberated by these [abandonments] and shall go to Śiva.
The seventeenth chapter, titled "The Section on Consciousness," is concluded;
now I shall explain the ritual procedure of Kālacakra in due order.
That which is known as Kālacakra is that by which time is awakened.
By moving for three days and nights, he lives for three years;
by moving for two days and nights, he shall live for two years.
By means of his movement through day and night, he lives for one year;
for him, one day passes and likewise one night.
"It is the certainty of the scriptures that death occurs after six months;
by following the second [method], he lives for a day and night."
Just as it is with Ādyā, so it is with Vāmā and likewise with Madhyamā;
this is declared to be Kālacakra, especially out of affection for my son.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Kālacakra," begins as previously promised: "The division of Śiva exists in eight ways."
O Lord of Gods, how might it be divided? Tell me this in truth, O Master.
They know [the letters] as *sakala*, *niṣkala*, *śūnya*, *kalāḍhya*, *khamalaṅkṛta*, *kṣapaṇa*, *antastha*, and the eighth is *kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*.
This verse is *Niḥśreyasamūla* 6:6 (f.21v,
l.2), with the reading *smṛtam* for *viduḥ*.
The palace (prāsāda), joined with the sixth [vowel] and endowed with the end of the sixth [group],
is proclaimed as the Śiva-tattva— entire and abiding in all beings.
The Lord himself, together with the vital breath (*samāruta*), departs after abandoning the body;
one should know that Śiva to be partless (*niṣkala*) and devoid of the six phonemes. (Stk_19.4)
Having abandoned inhalation and exhalation, one should remain in the body like a piece of wood;
one should recognize that state as empty and contemplate it with the heart. (Stk 19.5)
That reality which is proclaimed by means of the kissing face (cumbākāra) should be known as Kalāḍhya; now listen to that which resides in space. (Stk 19.6)

That which is proclaimed as the end of the upward-sounding [vibration] when it has subsided.
One should know that it resides there, adorned by space.
Turning his face away, he should speak thus to the Teacher of the World:
"It is called 'the destroyer of suffering' (kṣapaṇa); it is known as kṣapaṇa because of the destruction of that [suffering]. (Stk 19.8)
That which is proclaimed as the end of the diminished *adhonāda* should be known as the "residing at the end" (*antastha*); it is proclaimed to be unutterable. (Stk 19.9)
The eighth of the seven groups is the "peak" (koṭi); the second of the seventh;
that which exceeds the group and ends with six; and the third and fourth from the seventh. (Stk 19.10)
The first [syllable] should be joined again with the sixth of the first;
it is conjoined with Khaśekhara and is remembered as the eighth, consisting of the throat and labial sounds.
These divisions have been fully described for the accomplishment of the powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
that which is beyond utterance and free from doubt is designated as "liberation."
The nineteenth chapter, titled "The Section on the Exposition of the Eightfold Division of Śiva," begins:
How is he all-pervasive, and how does he exist below, above, and across?
Tell me this in its true essence out of compassion, O Maheśvara.
As long as it remains within the body of a living being, it is situated below;
once it has emerged, it pervades transversely; though remaining within, it is established everywhere.
The God who abides in the three paths exists within all bodies;
one is not liberated by failing to know this, even if there were absorption into him.
Therein, this threefold path with its three bases exists within all bodies;
he who knows this pervasion is undoubtedly all-pervading.
He does not undergo birth from a womb, as the Lord declares;
he wanders in saṃsāra only so long as he has not attained pervasion.
Having realized that the living soul is all-pervasive, one is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Just as a caterpillar reaches the tip of a blade of grass, so does the soul reach its destination.
Just as that which is above is without support, so too the living being (jīva) is situated here;
it is empty above, empty below, and empty within the interior of the body.
O Guha, he who understands the triple emptiness is certainly liberated;
its pervasiveness has been declared by me in brief, but not in detail.
Beyond this, there is no other pervader of the pervader.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Section on Pervasion" (Vyāptiprakaraṇa).
Hereafter, I shall explain how the conviction [of pervasion] is eightfold.
Likewise, there was the kindling of fire without fuel and the touching of trees.
It is the paralyzing of nooses, the destruction of great sins,
the neutralization of poison, and likewise the rendering [of enemies] seedless.
The destruction of the fever of the planets is known as the eightfold proof;
having understood this according to the rule, renown arises everywhere.
The syllable *ha* situated in the middle of the fire, likewise *hrīṃ*,
with *oṃ* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, is beneficial for one who does not maintain a sacrificial fire.
Having joined the fire with the stream and combined it with a thousand upward thrusts, through the application of the five-syllable mantra, it surely blazes forth; of this there is no doubt.
The syllable Oṃ is at the very bottom, and the letter Ra is situated above it;
when joined together as before, this practice is difficult to find on earth.
A tree, struck by seven hundred blows, dies;
its restoration, however, depends upon its being situated in a watery current.
That tree lives again just as it was before;
it is exactly the same once more, only deprived of the letter *r*.
For in the rite of nourishment, this [mantra] is illuminated by five drops,
joined with the letter *au* in its middle, and illumined at the end by the *praṇava*.
Beginning with the vowel *ī*, followed by *ha* in the middle, and then the center of fire (*ra*) thereafter—
this application at the time of the equinox causes the paralysis of the fetters.
With five hundred upward breaths, he certainly falls; there is no doubt.
Now listen to how his raising up occurs once again.
Joined with the letter *ī* at the beginning and end, with *hau* placed in the middle,
illuminated by the *anusvāra* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), ending with *namaḥ*, and followed again by the *praṇava*.
The knower of reality should employ the rite of awakening among all beings;
it should be applied with effort using exactly that many upward strokes.
The seed-syllable *la* is occupied by the individual soul (*jīva*), situated between the letters *ha* and *kṣa*;
it is positioned in the center as before, and is endowed with the wind (*vāyu*) and the bindu.
Just as it was explained that heaviness arises upon its ascent,
I shall explain once more how lightness arises.
The syllable Oṃ with the letter Ya becomes Haṃ; likewise, the syllable Au with Nam becomes Haṃ.
This is the Tulāpuruṣa yoga, performed with ten thousand exhalations.
That syllable *ha* is illuminated by the syllables *va* and *ya*;
with *hya* in the middle and *hlīṃ namaḥ* at the end, it is indeed the Vāruṇa mantra for the wise.
By means of exactly eight hundred suppressions, one certainly destroys poison,
just as it is seen that when fire blazes, it renders [the fuel] seedless.
In this case, a distinction is prescribed by means of five hundred suppressions (udghātas):
having placed the syllable Oṃ at the beginning, the syllable Hrūṃ follows immediately thereafter.
The mantra *hrauṃ hrūṃ ca phaṇṇamaḥ* is intended for the destruction of the planets at its conclusion;
it should be employed on the path of Varuṇa with eight hundred upward breaths (*udghāta*).
Then, beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), the wise one should likewise utter *huṃ phaṭ*, *huṃ phaṭ*, *huṃ phaṭ*,
and *phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ* using the water-mantra (*vāruṇa*).
By means of exactly eight hundred such exhalations (*udghāta*), he quickly destroys fever.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Section on Conditions," concerns the temple:
what kind of temple is to be known, and what is its pervasiveness?
O Maheśvara, tell me, what is his body like?
He who does not know the palace (prāsāda), which is the great body of the five mantras and endowed with thirty-eight kalās, is not called an ācārya.
If a guru bestows initiation without having correctly understood the temple (prāsāda), he leads both his disciple and himself downward; of this there is no doubt.
That teacher who, residing within the tip of the lotus of the temple, bestows initiation,
shall attain union with Śiva together with his disciple.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, Candra, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, as well as Āditya, Śukra, Skanda, and Bhṛgu.
And whatever other living beings there are, all the gods are said to be born of grace;
these and many other sages of rigid vows [are likewise so].
They meditate upon the supreme Haṃsa, the palace beyond name and form;
and I shall explain its division, by meditating upon which one attains the immortal.
They know that which is produced from the syllable *A* as being immediately joined with the eight digits (*kalā*).
One should know that the *Vāma* [mantra] is born from the syllable *U*, and the *Aghora* is born from the syllable *Ma*.
The person born from the seed-syllable (bindu) is to be known as Īśāna, who is born from the crest (śikhā).
Thus, these five mantras arise from the Prāsāda.
Ten billion mantras of immeasurable power have all been accomplished through the desired grace; of this there is no doubt.
The nine mantras beginning with Śakti that have been proclaimed as the Marutas are all born from the Prasāda and the Lotus, and they all possess unfailing power.
The Earth is to be known as Sadyojāta, while Water is proclaimed as Vāmadeva; Fire is said to be Aghora, and Wind is remembered as Tatpuruṣa.
Space, however, is the Lord; he himself is the god Maheśvara.
Sadyojāta is the Ṛgveda, and Vāmadeva is remembered as the Yajurveda.
Aghora is the Sāmaveda; Atharva is remembered as Puruṣa;
but the fifth is the supreme, subtle Sadāśiva, who pervades the ether.
Sadyojāta is indeed Brahmā; Vāma is proclaimed as Viṣṇu;
Aghora has Rudra as its presiding deity; and Īśvara is remembered as Puruṣa.
Īśāna has Śiva as his presiding deity and is situated in the heart and other locations;
he is the sixth supreme reality, established through qualities that are beyond comparison.
Having known the supreme ladder that leads to the fivefold abode, one should not describe his body as being produced from the qualities of material nature.
That very state which has been known once expands;
at that very moment one is liberated, for when that state is known, it is so.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "The Section on the Determination of Temples.
Listen, O Six-faced One, to the unsurpassed nectar of knowledge according to its true nature.
That which has not been told to anyone, nor should it be told—that I shall now declare.
Residing in the body, it is to be known as *sakala* (with parts); devoid of the body, it is *niṣkala* (without parts).
It is accessible through the instruction of a realized teacher; it abides everywhere as something indefinable.
He who says "Haṃsa, Haṃsa"—the god Haṃsa is Sadāśiva;
he is obtained directly from the mouth of the Guru, facing in all directions.
Just as oil resides in sesame seeds and fragrance in a flower,
so does the Puruṣa abide within this body, both externally and internally.
Just as someone with a torch in hand might discard it after having illuminated an object,
so too, having illuminated the knowable through knowledge, one should relinquish that knowledge.
One should know that the flower is the manifest (sakala), while its fragrance is the unmanifest (niṣkala); one should know that the tree is the manifest, while its shadow is the unmanifest.
The manifest state is both with parts and without parts, established everywhere;
likewise, the means is with parts, while the goal is indeed without parts.
In the differentiated state, all existence is differentiated; likewise, in the undifferentiated state, it is undifferentiated.
It is three measures, two measures, and likewise one measure.
The half-mora is supreme and subtle; beyond it is that which is higher than the highest.
Therein reside Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, or indeed Śiva himself.
The Sakala is recited as fivefold, having five deities:
Brahmā resides in the heart, and Viṣṇu is established in the throat.
Rudra resides in the middle of the palate; Maheśvara resides in the forehead;
one should know Śiva to be at the tip of the nose, and the supreme state is at its end.
At the tip of the nose (nāsāgra) according to MSS i, ī, u, and mu; at the end of the sound (nādānta) according to Bhaṭṭa.
"There is nothing higher than the Supreme"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
How does its coming and going occur, or by what is it led?
I have a doubt, O Mahādeva; tell it to me according to the truth:
by what power is the individual soul led, and having reached that [state], does it return?
I shall explain its limit to you; listen, O Six-faced One, according to the truth:
one should know that it transcends the body at a distance of twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose.
One should know that [the breath] ends there; stationed there, the Lord pervades all.
Even when the mind is cast elsewhere and the eye is directed elsewhere, [He remains].
Nevertheless, the yoga of yogins proceeds without interruption;
this is that supreme secret, this is that supreme syllable.
"There is nothing higher than this, nothing more auspicious than this,
and no knowledge higher than this," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Having obtained the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, the determination of the supreme syllable has been briefly, and not at length, declared by the God of gods.
This true nature of Śiva has issued from the mouth of Śiva;
it is the secret of secrets, the most profound mystery, which must be concealed with great effort.
It should never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has no son;
it should be given to one who is devoted to the guru, the gods, and the sacred fire, and who is constantly intent upon liberation.
This scripture should be bestowed [only upon the worthy]; one should not cause it to be given to others.
The giver of this goes to hell, and it shall never attain success [for him].
This nectar of Śiva has been declared by me; this is the truth, the very truth for you.
Having understood this, the wise man should wander at his ease.
Whether he be a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
wherever the man of knowledge who knows the supreme syllable always abides, [he remains established].
One who is attached to sense objects and remains a subject of worldly experience goes to Śiva at the end of the body;
indeed, by this very knowledge of the scripture, even a human being in any state whatsoever [attains it].
He is not tainted by merits or sins such as the killing of a Brahmin or the horse sacrifice;
he is remembered as the impeller, the awakener, and the supreme bestower of liberation.
Thus, the teacher on this earth should be known as being of three kinds:

the instigator (codaka) who shows the path, the awakener (bodhaka) who points out the state, and the giver of liberation (mokṣada) who [reveals] the supreme reality, knowing which one attains immortality. (Stk 23.26)
